hook.line: A customer swears Altamira has a judge in its pocket, and Tomás would rather not call anyone a liar. Spanish has a ladder of phrases for doubting a claim, from a polite shrug to an open challenge.
hook.es: No tengo tan claro que sea la mejor solución.
hook.en: I'm not so sure it's the best solution.

examples.es: No tengo tan claro que sea la mejor solución.
examples.en: I'm not so sure it's the best solution.

examples.es: Pongo en duda que el senador diga la verdad.
examples.en: I question whether the senator is telling the truth.

examples.es: Cuestiono que esa sea la causa.
examples.en: I question whether that's the cause.

examples.es: No tengo tan claro que Altamira tenga el permiso.
examples.en: I'm not so sure that Altamira has the permit.

examples.es: Tengo mis dudas de que sea verdad.
examples.en: I have my doubts that it's true.

examples.es: No me convence del todo ese plan.
examples.en: That plan doesn't entirely convince me.

rule:
These phrases let you doubt a claim without calling anyone a liar.

Softest: *No me convence del todo* and *tengo mis dudas*. In the middle: *no tengo tan claro que*. Strongest: *pongo en duda que* and *cuestiono que*, which openly challenge the claim.

After *que* the verb takes the wish form: *sea*, *tenga*, *diga*. You doubt it, so you do not state it.

Take the *no* away and you are sure: *tengo claro que Altamira tiene el permiso*, with the plain verb.
smallPrint: Teachers call this the subjunctive after expressions of doubt, which run from mild (*tengo mis dudas*) to strong (*cuestiono que*).

readAndPick.es: No tengo tan claro que sea la mejor solución.
options: I'm sure it's the best solution.
I'm not so sure it's the best solution.
It was the best solution.

readAndPick.es: Pongo en duda que el senador diga la verdad.
options: I'm sure the senator is telling the truth.
The senator questions whether I am telling the truth.
I question whether the senator is telling the truth.

readAndPick.es: Tengo claro que Altamira tiene el permiso.
options: I'm clear that Altamira has the permit.
I'm not so sure that Altamira has the permit.
I doubt that Altamira will get the permit.

readAndPick.es: Cuestiono que esa sea la causa.
options: I know that's the cause.
I question whether that's the cause.
She questions whether that's the cause.

readAndPick.es: No tenemos tan claro que Vale esté de acuerdo.
options: We're not so sure that Vale agrees.
I'm not so sure that Vale agrees.
They're sure that Vale agrees.

readAndPick.es: Tengo mis dudas de que sea verdad.
options: I'm sure it's true.
I have no doubts that it's true.
I have my doubts that it's true.

readAndPick.es: No me convence del todo ese plan.
options: That plan convinces me completely.
That plan doesn't entirely convince me.
I didn't entirely convince them of that plan.

readAndPick.es: No tengo tan claro que Altamira tenga el permiso.
options: I'm not so sure that Altamira has the permit.
I'm clear that Altamira has the permit.
Altamira is not so sure that I have the permit.

yourTurn.prompt: Pick and type the whole sentence: *No tengo tan claro que ___ la mejor solución.* (*es* or *sea*) I'm not so sure it's the best solution.
yourTurn.answer: No tengo tan claro que sea la mejor solución.
yourTurn.why: You doubt it, so the verb takes the wish form: *sea*.

yourTurn.prompt: Pick and type the whole sentence: *Pongo en duda que el senador ___ la verdad.* (*dice* or *diga*) I question whether the senator is telling the truth.
yourTurn.answer: Pongo en duda que el senador diga la verdad.
yourTurn.why: Questioning a claim is doubting it, so *diga*.

yourTurn.prompt: Say: I question whether that's the cause.
yourTurn.answer: Cuestiono que esa sea la causa.
yourTurn.why: *Cuestiono que* is a direct challenge, followed by the wish form *sea*.

yourTurn.prompt: Say: I'm not so sure that Altamira has the permit.
yourTurn.answer: No tengo tan claro que Altamira tenga el permiso.
yourTurn.why: *No tengo tan claro que* is followed by *tenga*, the wish form of *tener*.

yourTurn.prompt: Say: We're not so sure that Vale agrees.
yourTurn.answer: No tenemos tan claro que Vale esté de acuerdo.
yourTurn.why: *Tenemos* is the "we" form and *esté* is the wish form.

yourTurn.prompt: Turn *Es verdad* into a doubt, softly: I have my doubts that it's true.
yourTurn.answer: Tengo mis dudas de que sea verdad.
yourTurn.why: *Tengo mis dudas de que* is the gentlest doubt, and still takes *sea*.

yourTurn.prompt: Say it mildly: That plan doesn't entirely convince me.
yourTurn.answer: No me convence del todo ese plan.
accept: Ese plan no me convence del todo.
yourTurn.why: *No me convence del todo* needs no *que*, so no wish form is needed.

pitfalls.wrong: No tengo tan claro que es la mejor solución.
pitfalls.right: No tengo tan claro que sea la mejor solución.
pitfalls.why: Almost. You are doubting, so the verb after *que* takes the wish form.

pitfalls.wrong: Pongo en duda de que el senador diga la verdad.
pitfalls.right: Pongo en duda que el senador diga la verdad.
pitfalls.why: Almost. *Poner en duda* takes *que* directly, with no *de*.

pitfalls.wrong: Tengo claro que Altamira tenga el permiso.
pitfalls.right: Tengo claro que Altamira tiene el permiso.
pitfalls.why: Almost. Without *no* you are sure, so the verb stays plain.

personal: Think of a claim you have heard lately that you are not sure about. Doubt it politely with *no tengo tan claro que*, then say it more firmly with *pongo en duda que*.
